function.name: evolve_creatures
function.description: Apply the Evolutionary Algorithm to improve the creatures in a simulation over generations. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

population_size.description: The initial size of the creature population.

mutation_rate.description: The probability of mutation in each generation. This is a float type value.

generations.description: The number of generations to run the simulation.

fitness_goal.description: The fitness goal that the creatures should strive for. This is an optional parameter. Default: 1

message.content:
Below is a practical “cook‑book” for turning an evolutionary algorithm (EA) into a working AI system inside a video game. I’ll walk you through the whole pipeline—from encoding a character’s behaviour to running the evolution in real time—then give you a minimal but runnable Python example (using the popular **DEAP** framework). --- ## 1. Why use an EA in games? | Goal | Why an EA helps | |------|----------------| | **Procedural content** | Evolve level layouts, enemy placements, item distributions, etc. | | **Adaptive difficulty** | Continuously tune NPC behaviours so they stay challenging but not impossible. | | **Learning from players** | Use player data as part of the fitness signal to create more engaging experiences. | | **Exploration of creative solutions** | Find novel strategies or designs that human designers might miss. | EAs are especially useful when: * The search space is huge or poorly understood (e.g., neural network weights, rule sets). * You want *continuous* adaptation during gameplay. * You have a clear objective metric (score, survival time, win rate). --- ## 2. Core components of a game‑based EA | Component | What it does | Typical choices in a game context | |-----------|--------------|-----------------------------------| | **Genome / Individual** | Encodes a candidate solution (e.g., a set of parameters, a neural net, a decision tree). | • Float vector (weights)
• Bitstring (rule flags)
• Tree (behaviour tree) | | **Population** | A collection of individuals that will compete/evolve together. | Size 20–200 depending on computational budget. | | **Fitness Function** | Quantifies how good an individual is at the task. | • Game score
• Survival time
• Distance travelled
• Player satisfaction metrics | | **Selection** | Chooses parents based on fitness. | Tournament, roulette wheel, rank‑based. | | **Crossover / Recombination** | Combines two parents to produce offspring. | One‑point, uniform, subtree swap (for trees). | | **Mutation** | Randomly perturbs an individual to explore new areas. | Gaussian perturbation, bit flip, subtree replacement. | | **Replacement / Elitism** | Decides which individuals survive to next generation. | Keep best N (elitism), replace worst N. | | **Termination** | When to stop evolving. | Fixed generations, fitness threshold, no improvement after X gens. | --- ## 3. Step‑by‑step workflow ``` 1. Define the problem & objectives └─ Decide what you want the AI to learn (e.g., navigate maze, beat a boss) 2. Design the genome ├─ Choose representation (vector, tree, NN) └─ Set bounds/initial ranges 3. Build the fitness evaluator ├─ Wrap the game engine so you can instantiate an agent with a given genome └─ Run a simulation episode → return a scalar fitness 4. Initialize a random population └─ Sample genomes uniformly within bounds 5. Loop over generations: a. Evaluate all individuals (parallelise if possible) b. Select parents (tournament, etc.) c. Produce offspring via crossover + mutation d. Replace old population (elitism + new offspring) e. Log statistics (best fitness, diversity) 6. Deploy the best individual(s) └─ Load the winning genome into the live game (or keep evolving online) ``` ### Parallelisation tip Game simulations are often the bottleneck. Use multiprocessing or GPU‑accelerated simulators to evaluate many individuals concurrently. DEAP supports `multiprocessing.Pool` out of the box. --- ## 4. Example: Evolving a simple “run‑and‑jump” controller Let’s build a tiny demo where we evolve a controller that learns to jump over obstacles in a side‑scroller. We’ll use DEAP because it abstracts away most boilerplate. ```python # ------------------------------------------------------------ # 1️⃣ Install dependencies # pip install deap pygame numpy # ------------------------------------------------------------ import random import math import numpy as np import pygame from deap import base, creator, tools, algorithms # --------------------- 2️⃣ Game constants -------------------- SCREEN_W, SCREEN_H = 640, 480 FPS = 60 GRAVITY = 0.5 JUMP_VEL = -10 OBSTACLE_FREQ = 90 # frames between obstacles MAX_FRAMES = 500 # max frames per episode # --------------------- 3️⃣ Simple physics ------------------- class Agent: def __init__(self, genome): self.x, self.y = 50, SCREEN_H - 50 self.vel_y = 0 self.genome = genome # [threshold] – when to jump self.jump_threshold = genome[0] self.score = 0 def update(self): # Simple policy: jump if below threshold if self.y > self.jump_threshold: self.vel_y = JUMP_VEL self.vel_y += GRAVITY self.y += self.vel_y self.score += 1 def draw(self, surf): pygame.draw.rect(surf, (255,0,0), (self.x, int(self.y), 20, 30)) # --------------------- 4️⃣ Environment ---------------------- class Env: def __init__(self): self.obstacles = [] # list of rects self.frame_count = 0 def reset(self): self.obstacles.clear() self.frame_count = 0 def step(self, agent): self.frame_count += 1 # Add new obstacle if self.frame_count % OBSTACLE_FREQ == 0: y = SCREEN_H - random.randint(40, 120) self.obstacles.append(pygame.Rect(SCREEN_W, y, 20, SCREEN_H - y)) # Move obstacles left for obs in self.obstacles: obs.x -= 5 # Remove offscreen self.obstacles = [o for o in self.obstacles if o.right > 0] # Check collision agent_rect = pygame.Rect(agent.x, int(agent.y), 20, 30) for obs in self.obstacles: if agent_rect.colliderect(obs): return False # dead return True # alive def render(self, surf, agent): surf.fill((200,200,200)) agent.draw(surf) for obs in self.obstacles: pygame.draw.rect(surf, (0,0,0), obs) pygame.display.flip() # --------------------- 5️⃣ Fitness function ----------------- def eval_agent(individual): env.reset() agent = Agent(individual) alive = True while alive and env.frame_count < MAX_FRAMES: alive = env.step(agent) agent.update() return (agent.score,) # DEAP expects a tuple # --------------------- 6️⃣ DEAP setup ----------------------- creator.create("FitnessMax", base.Fitness, weights=(1.0,)) creator.create("Individual", list, fitness=creator.FitnessMax) toolbox = base.Toolbox() # Genome: single float threshold between 100 and 300 toolbox.register("attr_float", random.uniform, 100, 300) toolbox.register("individual", tools.initRepeat, creator.Individual, toolbox.attr_float, n=1) toolbox.register("population", tools.initRepeat, list, toolbox.individual) toolbox.register("evaluate", eval_agent) toolbox.register("mate", tools.cxBlend, alpha=0.5) toolbox.register("mutate", tools.mutGaussian, mu=0, sigma=20, indpb=0.5) toolbox.register("select", tools.selTournament, tournsize=3) # --------------------- 7️⃣ Main loop ------------------------ if __name__ == "__main__": pygame.init() screen = pygame.display.set_mode((SCREEN_W, SCREEN_H)) clock = pygame.time.Clock() env = Env() pop = toolbox.population(n=50) stats = tools.Statistics(lambda ind: ind.fitness.values) stats.register("avg", np.mean) stats.register("max", np.max) # Run evolution pop, log = algorithms.eaSimple(pop, toolbox, cxpb=0.5, mutpb=0.2, ngen=30, stats=stats, verbose=True) # Pick the best individual best_ind = tools.selBest(pop, k=1)[0] print("Best genome:", best_ind) # Demo the evolved agent agent = Agent(best_ind) running = True while running: for event in pygame.event.get(): if event.type == pygame.QUIT: running = False alive = env.step(agent) agent.update() env.render(screen, agent) clock.tick(FPS) if not alive: running = False pygame.quit() ``` **What this script does** 1. **Environment** – A very small side‑scrolling world with randomly placed platforms. 2. **Agent** – Has one parameter (`jump_threshold`) controlling when it jumps. 3. **Fitness** – Total frames survived (higher is better). 4. **Evolution** – Uses blend crossover, Gaussian mutation, tournament selection. 5. **Demo** – After training, runs the best individual until death. Feel free to replace the environment with your own game logic; just make sure `eval_agent` returns a numeric fitness. --- ## 5. Practical tips & common pitfalls | Issue | Fix / Recommendation | |-------|----------------------| | **Evaluation noise** | Average fitness over several episodes per individual. | | **Premature convergence** | Increase mutation rate, add diversity preservation (crowding distance). | | **Too slow evaluations** | Use a lightweight simulator or surrogate models (neural nets predicting fitness). | | **Hard to interpret results** | Visualise genomes (e.g., plot weight histograms) or log intermediate behaviours. | | **Integration latency** | Run evolution offline (pre‑compute a library of behaviours) or use incremental learning (online EA). | | **Parameter tuning** | Start with standard values (pop 50–200, cx 0.5, mut 0.2) then adjust based on observed progress. | --- ## 6. Going beyond simple controllers If you’re interested in more sophisticated AI, consider: | Technique | What it adds | |-----------|--------------| | **Neuroevolution** | Evolve neural networks (weights, topology). Libraries: NEAT-Python, TensorFlow‑GA. | | **Behaviour Trees** | Encode sub‑trees as genomes; crossover swaps sub‑trees. | | **Multi‑objective EA** | Optimize for both performance and resource usage (speed, memory). | | **Co‑evolution** | Simultaneously evolve opponents or environmental challenges. | | **Hybrid methods** | Combine EA with reinforcement learning (e.g., EA optimises hyperparameters for RL). | --- ## 7. Resources & further reading | Resource | Why it’s useful | |----------|-----------------| | **DEAP documentation** | Quick start guides, tutorials. | | **“An Introduction to Genetic Algorithms” (Mitchell)** | Classic textbook covering theory. | | **“Genetic Programming” (Koza)** | For evolving programs / trees. | | **OpenAI Gym + DEAP** | Many gym environments already support vectorised evaluation. | | **Unity ML‑Agents** | Provides a Python API that can be hooked into DEAP or other GA frameworks. | --- ### TL;DR 1. **Encode** the AI behaviour as a genome (vector, tree, NN). 2. **Define** a clear fitness metric (score, survival time, etc.). 3. **Wrap** the game so you can instantiate an agent from a genome and run a deterministic episode. 4. **Run** the EA loop (selection → crossover → mutation → replacement). 5. **Deploy** the best genome or keep evolving online. With the skeleton above you can plug in almost any game logic you like. Happy evolving!
